# Cache evaluation, 2026-11-27

Does the in-process `cache` component (access logic, per-user stream tree,
username lookups) still pay off now that the base storage is PostgreSQL or
per-user SQLite? This memo measures it, checks its invalidation paths, and
looks at what the `[FELT]` acceptance test actually proves.

**Recommendation: keep the cache as it is, active by default on both engines.**
It is a clear win on PostgreSQL (1.2x to 7.5x throughput on every measured
call) and a smaller but consistent one on SQLite (+18% to +38% on the calls
where the difference is outside the noise, and no call slower). Trimming it
to the access logic alone would lose most of the PostgreSQL gain. One
invalidation gap was found and fixed (`createDeleted`, below). The `[FELT]`
test's 15% threshold is not a reliable signal and should be reworked.

## What the cache holds and where it sits

- **Access logic** (`ACCESS_LOGICS_BY_USERID`): the `AccessLogic` of a token,
  by token and by id. Read by `MethodContext` on every authenticated call; a
  miss costs the access read from storage and the permission set build.
- **Stream tree** (`STREAMS`, store `local`): the user's full stream tree, as
  returned by the engine's `find` + `buildTree`. Read through
  `_getAllFromAccountAndCache` by every `streams.get` / `getOne` of the local
  store, on both engines.
- **Username to user id**: one lookup per request.

Entries expire after `caching:accessMaxAgeSeconds` (default 60 s, at most
300 s) and are busted across API workers by the synchro channel.

The stream tree is the part that matters most, and not only between
requests. Without it, every `getOne` / `getOneWithNoChildren` loads and builds
the whole tree again. The access logic walks up parent chains with one such
call per step, and `events.get` resolves its stream query through
`streams.get`, so a single call made with a restricted token reads the whole
stream table several times when the cache is off (counted below). With the
cache on, that becomes one read per user and API worker, per invalidation or
per max age.

## Method

- Machine: 8-core x86_64 Linux box, idle apart from the run. Node 24.22.3,
  the bundled PostgreSQL 16 and rqlite, open-pryv.io master at `3aa9dd30`.
- One core started with `bin/master.js` (2 API workers, the default),
  `trace` and log output off, `caching:isActive` set to `true` or `false`
  in `override-config.yml`, the core restarted between the two.
- Data: `tools/performance/datasets/seed.js`, `manual` profile (68 streams,
  some nested 4 deep), 2 users, about 13 000 (PostgreSQL) and 16 000 (SQLite)
  events each, a `shared` access with `contribute` on 10 leaf streams (the
  "restricted" token) and the personal token.
- A small client (Node `fetch`, keep-alive) runs each call for 8 s at
  concurrency 1 (latency) and 10 s at concurrency 10 (throughput), after a
  3 s warm-up. Calls:
  - `access-info` (restricted token): the access-logic path alone;
  - `streams.get` (personal and restricted);
  - `events.get` with `limit=20` (restricted) and `limit=500` (personal);
  - `events.create` (restricted): no cache invalidation;
  - `streams.update` rename (personal): busts the user's streams and access
    logic in every worker;
  - mixed: one stream rename every 10 requests, the other 9 are restricted
    `streams.get`, only the reads timed: the read path under steady
    invalidation.
- 3 repetitions per engine and mode, on/off order alternated per repetition
  (on-off, off-on, on-off) so slow drift does not favour one mode. Tables show
  the median of the 3 runs and the min-max range. A difference is called real
  when the on and off ranges do not overlap.

## Results: PostgreSQL

Concurrency 1 (median p50 latency, ms; median throughput, req/s):

| call | p50 on | p50 off | req/s on | req/s off | on vs off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| access-info | 1.2 | 3.2 | 588 | 265 | +122% |
| streams.get personal | 2.9 | 6.7 | 305 | 144 | +112% |
| streams.get restricted | 2.4 | 7.1 | 364 | 137 | +166% |
| events.get 20, restricted | 5.6 | 44.1 | 168 | 22.5 | +647% |
| events.get 500, personal | 23.6 | 38.0 | 41.7 | 26.2 | +59% |
| events.create, restricted | 10.6 | 13.5 | 93 | 67 | +39% |
| streams.update rename | 9.0 | 12.4 | 94 | 73 | +28% |
| mixed reads, 10% renames | 2.4 | 7.2 | 247 | 114 | +116% |

Concurrency 10:

| call | p50 on | p50 off | req/s on | req/s off | on vs off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| access-info | 10.7 | 15.0 | 634 | 546 | +16% |
| streams.get personal | 17.9 | 31.7 | 420 | 302 | +39% |
| streams.get restricted | 17.1 | 31.7 | 488 | 296 | +65% |
| events.get 20, restricted | 24.0 | 195.9 | 372 | 50 | +646% |
| events.get 500, personal | 103.8 | 165.6 | 96 | 58.5 | +63% |
| events.create, restricted | 19.9 | 36.6 | 432 | 263 | +64% |
| streams.update rename | 31.0 | 45.0 | 298 | 219 | +36% |
| mixed reads, 10% renames | 16.5 | 31.4 | 387 | 261 | +48% |

No range overlaps between on and off on PostgreSQL: every difference above is
real. Run-to-run spread was small (typically under 5% of the median).

| streams.update rename | 3.5 | 4.0 | 231 | 215 | +7% (ranges overlap) |
| mixed reads, 10% renames | 2.5 | 3.6 | 290 | 211 | +37% |

Concurrency 10:

| call | p50 on | p50 off | req/s on | req/s off | on vs off |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| access-info | 8.7 | 12.4 | 761 | 630 | +21% |
| streams.get personal | 14.2 | 19.8 | 543 | 445 | +22% |
| streams.get restricted | 15.7 | 20.8 | 536 | 433 | +24% |
| events.get 20, restricted | 254 | 198 | 39 | 50 | noise |
| events.get 500, personal | 109 | 126 | 91 | 79 | +15% (ranges overlap) |
| events.create, restricted | 16.9 | 22.3 | 467 | 382 | +22% |
| streams.update rename | 17.6 | 23.0 | 471 | 392 | +20% |
| mixed reads, 10% renames | 15.4 | 20.4 | 458 | 387 | +18% |

The two `events.get` rows are dominated by something other than the cache:
the restricted `limit=20` call went from 14 ms to 55 ms over the session and
back to 16 ms on the last run, whatever the cache mode, as the events written
by the `events.create` runs accumulated in the queried stream; the first
`limit=500` run after seeding was 4 times slower than all later ones. Those
rows say nothing about the cache either way. Every other SQLite difference is
outside the run-to-run ranges.

## Invalidation cost

A stream write busts the user's stream tree and access logic in every worker,
so the next request of that user pays the full reload. Measured directly:

- `streams.update` itself is not slower with the cache on: it is faster
  (PostgreSQL +28% / +36%, SQLite +7% / +20%), because the method's own
  access and stream checks hit the cache before the bust.
- With one rename every 10 requests, the reads in between are still 2.2x
  (PostgreSQL) and 1.4x (SQLite) faster at concurrency 1 than with no cache:
  one reload per invalidation is far cheaper than one or more reloads on every
  request.

So the invalidation cost does not outweigh the gain even for a write-heavy
stream workload; it would take renames on most requests for the cache to stop
paying.

## Why the PostgreSQL gap is so large: stream table reads per request

Reads of the PostgreSQL `streams` table (`seq_scan + idx_scan` from
`pg_stat_user_tables`) over a few hundred requests of each call, concurrency 1:

| call | reads per request, cache off | cache on |
|---|---|---|
| access-info | 0 | 0 |
| streams.get restricted | 1.0 | 0 |
| events.get 20, restricted | 13.9 | 0 |
| events.get 500, personal | 5.1 | 0 |
| events.create, restricted | 2.1 | 1.0 |

Each read without the cache is a full-table read plus `buildTree`; a restricted
`events.get` does about 14 of them (permission checks walking parent chains,
then the stream query). The one read left on `events.create` with the cache on
is the indexed lookup of the stream's path in the events storage, not a tree
load. On SQLite the same reloads happen but come from a small local file, which
is why the SQLite gains are smaller.

## Invalidation correctness

Every write path of the local streams store was read for its cache bust:

- `insertOne`, `updateOne`, `delete` (both engines' `Streams*` storage) and
  `deleteAll` bust after the write completes, unconditionally; the epoch fence
  in `setStreams` drops a fill whose storage read straddled a bust. Moving a
  stream in or out of an access's scope is covered by `[XDP6]`.
- `create` removing an earlier deletion record (`removeOne`) changes no live
  stream: no bust needed.
- **Gap found and fixed:** `createDeleted` (both engines) wrote the deletion
  record without busting. When the stream existed, it is marked deleted in
  storage while the cached tree still listed it until the max age. It is only
  reachable through `mall.streams.create` with a `deleted` timestamp, which
  the API schema does not accept (the test fixtures use it), so no API
  caller could hit it. Both engines now bust after
  that write too; test `[CDLB]` covers it (fails without the fix on both
  engines, passes with it).
- **Out of scope of the cache, noted:** a `bin/backup.js --restore
  --overwrite` run against a core that is serving the same account clears and
  rewrites its streams and accesses from a separate process, which sends no
  bust. The serving workers can then use the previous tree and access logic
  for up to `caching:accessMaxAgeSeconds`. Running such a restore with the
  account idle, or restarting the API workers after it, avoids it.
- Account deletion busts by user id (`unsetUserById`), access changes by
  access (`unsetAccessLogic`), renames and alias changes by name: unchanged by
  this review.

On the backlog question whether `setStreams` / `filterTree` overshoots on
engines that build the tree per query: `filterTree` copies the tree on every
`streams.get`, cached or not (the cached tree must not be handed out for
mutation), so it is paid on both paths; the cache only removes the storage
read and `buildTree`. It never makes a call slower in the measurements above.

## The `[FELT]` test

`[FELT]` times three `streams.get` calls on an empty cache ("first"), three on
a full cache ("second") and three with the cache off, all in-process, and
asserts that "second" is at least 15% faster than "off" (skipped under SQLite
and in CI). Sampled 10 times per engine, assertions disabled (mean of the
three calls, ms):

| engine | first | second | off | gain of second over off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | 10.7-11.2 | 4.5-5.1 | 6.6-7.1 | 24% to 36%, median 30% |
| SQLite | 8.6-8.7 | 4.5-5.0 | 4.3-5.7 | -14% to +17%, median 11% |

- PostgreSQL: the threshold holds with margin on this machine, but the test
  measures a single small tree with three samples per side, so on a slower or
  loaded runner it is one noisy sample away from failing (hence its retries
  and the CI opt-out).
- SQLite: the gain is inside the noise of three samples (4 of 10 runs
  negative), so the opt-out is right: the 15% assertion cannot hold there as
  written. The benchmark above still shows a real gain on SQLite under load;
  this test is too small to see it.
- "Off" is cheaper than "first": the first call also fills the access logic
  and username caches and starts following the user, so "first" is not a
  no-cache baseline either.

The functional part of the test (the cache is filled after a call, and the
second call is faster than the first) is sound on both engines. The timing
threshold proves little. A deterministic replacement would assert what the
cache is for, for instance that a second `streams.get` or a restricted
`events.get` makes no stream storage read, by counting calls to the streams
storage `find`, and drop the percentage.

## Recommendation

- **Keep the cache, active by default, on both engines.** PostgreSQL gains are
  large everywhere; SQLite gains are smaller (its per-user file reads are
  cheap) but consistent, and nothing measured got slower with the cache on.
- **Do not trim it to the access logic only.** On PostgreSQL the stream tree
  carries most of the gain (`streams.get` +112% to +166%, restricted
  `events.get` 7.5x), because without it the access logic and stream queries
  reload the tree several times per request.
- If the cache were ever removed, a per-request memo of the stream tree would
  be needed first, or restricted reads on PostgreSQL would slow down several
  times over.
- Rework `[FELT]` as described above.

## Reproducing

The client, the driver and the raw results are not kept in the repository.
The driver writes an `override-config.yml` per leg (engine, `caching.isActive`,
`setup.registrationWhilePending: open` so the seed can register users,
`service.eventTypes: file://test/event-types-flat.json`), runs
`tools/performance/datasets/seed.js`, then times the calls listed under
Method with Node `fetch`. `tools/performance` (`bin/run-benchmark.js`) can be
used the same way, run once per `caching.isActive` value.
